content:
Arthritis in the feet and ankles can make each step painful. People often shorten their steps, hold on more and walk less, which can reduce strength and balance over time.

This guide explains how foot pain and balance are linked and how to practise balance safely. It is educational information, not a personal exercise prescription.

Why painful feet affect balance

  • Pain changes how you place your feet and shift weight.
  • Stiff ankles and toes make it harder to correct a wobble.
  • Numbness or reduced feeling in the feet, for example from diabetes, affects balance.
  • Walking less leads to weaker legs.
  • Poorly fitting shoes or slippers add to the risk.

Practising balance safely

  • Stand next to a kitchen worktop or sturdy chair, with someone nearby if you are unsure.
  • Start with standing with feet slightly closer together, holding on lightly.
  • Try sit-to-stand from a firm chair.
  • Progress slowly and stop if pain is sharply worse or you feel dizzy.
  • Programmes such as Otago or strength and balance classes are often available locally.

Footwear and foot care

  • Choose shoes with a firm heel, cushioned sole, secure fastening and room for the toes.
  • Avoid backless slippers and walking in socks.
  • Keep nails and skin cared for, or ask for help.
  • Insoles or orthoses may be suggested by a podiatrist.

Getting help

Ask your GP about NHS podiatry, physiotherapy or a falls assessment if your feet are painful, you feel unsteady, or you have fallen. NICE guidance on falls recommends a multifactorial assessment for people at risk.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop walking if my feet hurt?

Not usually. Supportive shoes and pacing may help you keep walking. Ask for advice if pain is limiting you.

Can balance improve with arthritic feet?

Many people improve with regular, supported strength and balance practice.

Who do I ask about insoles?

Your GP can refer you to podiatry, or you can see a registered podiatrist.
